text: I like the farmers market because it has that quality. You go there early. So early that the stalls are not set up yet and then gradually more and more stalls come up. I was there at seven and there was about five or six stalls. And then by eight o'clock, it was full. It was just this square with all these little tents, white tents, just flapping in the wind. I was early. I brought my table and my tomatoes. Tomatoes that are not pretty. Tomatoes that have some spots and some cracked, but they smell delicious. I put them very nicely. I set them very nicely. And across from me, there is a lady who sells honey, very nice honey, yellow. She says hello to me, she waves. She says, you're late, the basil was already bought by the early ones. I say that's fine, I'm here for the quiet. But the quiet doesn't last very long. So soon, the square is full of people. You have a guitar player, you have somebody who is making coffee, a small little guy who's cutting some tomatoes or something. There's a girl that is sniffing at the honey, the jars of honey, she puts her nose to the glass and smells. There's a guy who is in a very nice linen apron who is negotiating with somebody about the price of chard. It smells of wet earth, it smells of cinnamon, of fried onions, of the smell of peach, of all these things. And I'm just sitting there with my tomatoes and watching people. I've been going to this market for 30 years, and I used to go there with my wife. We'd buy flowers. We'd buy sunflowers. We'd buy whatever. She would buy flowers even when we didn't have money for bread. She would buy flowers. Now I go alone. But I still expect that I will see her, I still expect to see her at the corner with sunflowers, just turning them around, just looking at the flower. And a boy came to my table, a little boy, maybe 9 years old, who had a little cowlick in his hair. He says, do you have these tomatoes? I said yes. He says they're ugly. I said yeah, they're ugly. But they taste nice, like the ones that your grandmother used to grow. He said, my grandmother doesn't grow tomatoes, she grows roses. I said yes, but she would know. And he bought two tomatoes and he took them very carefully, like they were eggs. And then the wind changed and it smelled like rain. And everybody started looking up at the sky. And the lady covered her honey jars, etc. And the guitar player was playing, singing some songs about rivers. And then slowly, slowly, at noon, everybody started leaving. I sold almost all my tomatoes. I packed my boxes, I folded my table. And I just stood there for a minute. And I walked past the flower lady and I saw the sunflowers in a bucket outside. And I saw this little girl with yellow boots again holding one sunflower. And her mom was laughing, just laughing about something that the guy said. And I stood there and I was just looking at it. I don't buy flowers anymore. I stopped buying flowers. I thought it was a waste of money. Or a betrayal, I don't know. But I looked at it and I thought of what my wife used to say. She used to say the market is just a kitchen with no walls. And then I just bought one sunflower. I don't know why, I just bought it. And I took it home, the sunflower just touching my face, my shoulder. And I put it in a glass of water in my kitchen. And I sat there and looked at it for a long time. And it was getting darker and darker and darker. And I just sat there looking at it, just looking at the market, just looking at her, just looking at all of it. And it was very nice.
